To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spontaneous waves of action potential activity in the retina drive correlated bursts of action potential activity within the LGN.
spontaneous retinal waves are transmitted to the LGN, where they drive bursts of action potentials, and the transmission is not dependent on NMDA receptors.
the spontaneous waves of action potential discharge produced by the developing retina are transmitted to the thalamus, where they drive bursts of action potentials in thalamic neurons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of spontaneous activity in the development of the visual system.
how the brain develops its initial wiring pattern, and the role of activity in this process.
understanding how the visual system is wired up.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thalamus receives spontaneous retinal activity and transmits this activity to the cortex.
spontaneous activity in the retina drives correlated firing in the LGN.
the retinal waves are relayed to the LGN and that this relay is important for the development of visual cortex and the formation of the thalamocortical synapse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spontaneous retinal activity is transmitted to the LGN and drives the firing of action potentials.

the spontaneous activity of retinal ganglion neurons is not only important for retinotectal development and retinotectum synaptic refinement, but also for retinogeniculate synapse development and retinogeniculate refinement.
spontaneous activity in the retina is relayed to the LGN, which could influence the development of the cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the retina is not silent before vision.
the retina is not just a light sensor, it is an active participant in the development of visual circuits.
